claims.text: The pre-exposure Q235 steel has only its native oxide film and no additional surface treatment.
An engineered surface coating can promote formation of a uniform, continuous passive oxide layer on Q235 steel.
The engineered coating will suppress corrosion-related degradation relative to untreated Q235 steel at both room and elevated temperatures.
A phosphate-doped conversion coating can function as a corrosion-inhibiting treatment.
The intervention will produce a dense, protective passive film.
The resulting passive oxide layer will be uniform and defect-free.
The protective coating minimizes direct contact between the corrosive medium and the steel substrate.
Reduced contact between the medium and substrate reduces corrosion-related electrochemical reactions.
The coating reduces development of corrosion-accelerating micro-galvanic cells.
Coated Q235 steel will have a lower corrosion rate than untreated Q235 steel.
Coated samples will exhibit less mass loss than untreated samples.
Coated samples will exhibit slower pitting initiation than untreated samples.
Coated samples will exhibit lower corrosion current density than untreated samples.
The protective effect is contingent on the coating remaining fully intact.
Extreme temperature, prolonged exposure, or mechanical damage may reduce or eliminate protection by compromising film integrity.

contradictions.description: The boundary conditions make protection conditional on the coating remaining intact, but the falsification rule treats failure of the layer to remain intact as falsification. Film failure could instead place the experiment outside the stated applicability boundary, so the decisive test should separately require an intact coating when evaluating the proposed barrier mechanism.
